issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, can go into the question of the sufficiency of the material which had satisfied the Magistrate to initiate proceedings under Section 145(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: A Magistrate initiated proceedings under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure after receiving an application from the appellant and examining the appellant on oath.
The High Court, in its revisional jurisdiction, set aside the Magistrate's order.

One of the reasons for the High Court's decision was that the Magistrate had acted only on the allegations in the appellant's application without further enquiry, implying the material was insufficient.
law: The satisfaction required under Section 145(1) to initiate proceedings is that of the Magistrate.
The decision of whether the materials presented are sufficient to initiate proceedings is within the Magistrate's discretion.
The law allows a Magistrate to initiate proceedings based on a police report or "other information," which is a broad term that includes an application by a private party.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Magistrate had expressed his satisfaction based on the facts in the application after examining the appellant on oath.
The Court determined that these facts were considered "prima facie sufficient" by the Magistrate and constituted the reasons for his satisfaction.
The Court held that the High Court's role in its revisional jurisdiction is not to re-evaluate or question the sufficiency of the material that satisfied the Magistrate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court, in exercising its revisional jurisdiction, cannot go into the question of the sufficiency of the material that satisfied the Magistrate to initiate proceedings. The satisfaction is a matter of the Magistrate's discretion, and as long as there is some material upon which the Magistrate could be satisfied, the High Court should not interfere.

issue.issue_text: Whether the completion of a forcible and wrongful dispossession before the date of the Magistrate's preliminary order means that there is no existing dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace, thereby ousting the Magistrate's jurisdiction under Section 145(1).

facts: A party (the appellant) was forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed of a property.
This act of dispossession was completed before the Magistrate passed a preliminary order under Section 145 on June 20, 1966.

The High Court had set aside the Magistrate's order, reasoning that since the dispossession was complete, there was no longer an existing dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace on the date of the order, thus removing the Magistrate's jurisdiction.
law: Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is designed to prevent breaches of the peace arising from disputes over immovable property.

The second proviso to Section 145(4) states that if a party has been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed within two months before the date of the preliminary order, the Magistrate may treat that party as if they were in possession on that date.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning to be incorrect because it completely ignored the purpose of the second proviso to Section 145(4).

The Court argued that if the High Court's view were accepted, it would mean that any party who successfully and quickly completes a forcible and wrongful dispossession would be rewarded for their illegal act. The victim would be left without the speedy remedy of Section 145 simply because the wrong was already complete.

The Court explained that the second proviso was specifically introduced to address these exact situations. It creates a legal fiction, allowing the Magistrate to 'deem' the wrongfully dispossessed person to be in possession on the date of the order, provided the dispossession occurred within the preceding two months.

Therefore, even though the dispossession was a completed act, the dispute over possession still existed. The fact that the dispossession occurred within the two-month statutory period brought the case squarely within the Magistrate's jurisdiction under the second proviso.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view. It held that the completion of a forcible and wrongful dispossession before the Magistrate's preliminary order does not oust the Magistrate's jurisdiction. The second proviso to Section 145(4) was precisely enacted to cover such scenarios, allowing the Magistrate to treat the dispossessed party as being in possession and proceed with the case to prevent a breach of the peace and to ensure that a wrongdoer does not benefit from their illegal actions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the completion of a forcible and wrongful dispossession before the date of the Magistrate's preliminary order means that there is no existing dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace, thereby ousting the Magistrate's jurisdiction under Section 145(1).
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that despite being forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed on June 11, 1966, he should be deemed to be in possession on the date of the preliminary order (June 20, 1966) under the second proviso to Section 145(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Therefore, the Magistrate had jurisdiction to hear the matter and restore possession.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that since the dispossession of the appellant was a completed act before the Magistrate's preliminary order, there was no existing dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace, and therefore the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction under Section 145(1).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The satisfaction of a Magistrate to initiate proceedings under s. 145(1) is a matter of discretion, and a High Court in its revisional jurisdiction will not examine the sufficiency of the material that satisfied the Magistrate. Furthermore, under the second proviso to s. 145(4), a party who is forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed must be deemed to be in possession on the date of the preliminary order, as such an act of dispossession is not recognized as complete under criminal law.
obiter: The jurisdiction under s. 145 is of an emergency nature, and a Magistrate must act with caution.
No hard and fast rule can be laid down as to the sufficiency of material for the Magistrate's satisfaction.
The proviso is founded on the principle that forcible and wrongful dispossession is not to be recognised under the criminal law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred in interfering with the Magistrate's order. The satisfaction of a Magistrate to initiate proceedings under Section 145(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a discretionary matter based on prima facie materials, and a High Court in its revisional capacity cannot question the sufficiency of those materials. Furthermore, the court held that a forcible and wrongful dispossession completed before the Magistrate's preliminary order does not oust the Magistrate's jurisdiction, as the second proviso to Section 145(4) was specifically enacted to address such situations by deeming the dispossessed party to be in possession, thereby ensuring that a wrongdoer does not benefit from their unlawful act.
legal_tests_applied: The satisfaction under sub-s. (1) of s. 145 is that of the Magistrate. The question whether on the materials before him he should initiate proceedings or not is, therefore, in his discretion.
The High Court in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction would not go into the question of sufficiency of material which had satisfied the Magistrate.

The second proviso to sub-s. (4) of Section 145 was introduced precisely to meet cases of forcible and wrongful dispossession, allowing a Magistrate to treat the dispossessed party as if they were in possession on the date of the preliminary order if the dispossession occurred within two months prior.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the High Court could review the sufficiency of the material before the Magistrate was rejected because the satisfaction under Section 145(1) is a matter of the Magistrate's discretion, which is not to be interfered with in revision on the grounds of sufficiency.

The respondent's argument that a completed dispossession before the preliminary order meant there was no existing dispute likely to cause a breach of peace was rejected. The court reasoned that this view 'does not take into consideration the second proviso to sub-s. (4) which was introduced precisely to meet such cases' and would wrongly deny the benefit of Section 145 to a party who was forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed.
policy_considerations: The proviso to Section 145(4) is founded on the principle that forcible and wrongful dispossession is not to be recognised under the criminal law.

To hold that a completed dispossession ousts the Magistrate's jurisdiction 'would mean that if a party who is forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed does not in retaliation take the law into his hands, he should be at a disadvantage and cannot have the benefit of s. 145.'
